citation: Cheval, Boris, Matthew W. Miller, Dan Orsholits, Tanya Berry, David Sander, and Matthieu P. Boisgontier. "Physically Active Individuals Look for More: An Eye-Tracking Study of Attentional Bias." Psychophysiology 57, no. 6 (2020): e13582. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.13582.
discipline: health/exercise psychology, affective science (attentional-bias methodology); NOT a boredom study
boredom_engagement: NONE -- a full-text search of the extracted manuscript for 'bored'/'boredom' or any cognate term returns zero hits. The paper studies attentional bias toward physical-activity vs. physical-inactivity picture stimuli as a function of usual physical-activity level. It is retained in Strand E purely for its measure-axis value (eye-tracking + pupillometry + behavioral RT within one dot-probe paradigm). All construct-axis links in this entry are explicitly flagged analogical readings supplied by the corpus builder, not claims present in the source.
thesis: Cheval, Miller, Orsholits, Berry, Sander, and Boisgontier identify a gap in exercise psychology: prior attentional-bias research on physical activity relied almost entirely on indirect, reaction-time-based paradigms (Stroop, dot-probe), and only one prior study (Giel et al., 2013, in anorexia nervosa patients and athletes) had used eye-tracking for a more direct measure. The authors pair a visual dot-probe task with an eye tracker in 77 healthy young adults spanning low to high usual physical-activity levels, using reaction time (indirect), first-gaze location and gaze duration (direct visual-attention indices), and pupil dilation (arousal/value index) as four dependent measures. Four hypotheses predict that more physically active participants will (H1) detect a dot faster where a physical-activity image had been, (H2) look first toward physical-activity images, (H3) gaze longer at them, and (H4) show greater pupil dilation viewing them; an exploratory aim asks whether the eye-tracking/pupil indices predict reaction-time performance. H1-H3 were confirmed, conditional on moderate-to-high usual activity level; H4 was disconfirmed in direction (pupil size decreased, not increased, with relevance) and the effect was small enough that the authors caution against over-interpreting it.

sections.title: Title page, Impact statement, Abstract
sections.summary: Lay summary and structured abstract: eye tracking + dot-probe method, N=77, four dependent measures, headline results, variance explained (13.9%-40%).

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates a shift from reflective (attitude/intention) exercise-behavior theories toward automatic/impulsive-process accounts; defines attentional bias (Fadardi, Cox, & Rahmani, 2016); surveys prior paradigms (Stroop, dot-probe, spatial cuing, free viewing, visual search) and prior physical-activity attentional-bias findings; isolates the eye-tracking gap via Giel et al. (2013); states aim and four hypotheses.

sections.title: 2. Method
sections.summary: Participants/procedures (84 recruited, one-hour session, exclusion criteria, light-standardized cubicle); the visual dot-probe task (stimuli from Kullmann et al., 2014, Zenodo-hosted); usual physical activity via adapted IPAQ; statistical analysis (mixed-effects models, crossed random effects, multi-optimizer convergence, conditional pseudo-R2); the four outcome definitions; exploratory RT-prediction models.

sections.title: 3. Results
sections.summary: Descriptive statistics (final N=77); reaction times (H1); first gaze/H2, gaze duration/H3, pupil dilation/H4; predicting behavioral performance from eye-tracking outcomes.

sections.title: 4. Discussion
sections.summary: Interprets each hypothesis against prior literature (Giel et al., 2013; the Berry et al., 2011, gender discrepancy); situates attentional bias within reward-learning/incentive-salience accounts; lists strengths; names six limitations plus an 'outcome devaluation' confound.

sections.title: Conclusion through acknowledgements
sections.summary: Restates the headline finding; proposes attention-bias-modification treatment as a future intervention target (MacLeod et al., 2002); dedicates the paper to co-designer Remi Radel's memory.

sections.title: References; Tables and figure captions
sections.summary: ~55 references, overwhelmingly exercise-psychology/affective-science/addiction-neuroscience, none phenomenological or boredom-specific; Table 1 (participant characteristics), Table 2 (mixed-model coefficients), Figures 1-3 (task diagram, RT plot, eye-tracking plots).

measures.label: pupil dilation / pupillometry
measures.signal: difference in maximum pupil size per trial when viewing physical-activity vs. physical-inactivity stimuli
measures.apparatus: eye tracker (brand/model/sampling rate not specified in the extracted text); values <2mm or >4.5mm excluded, active-inactive differences >|1|mm excluded; linear mixed model (participants + stimuli as crossed random effects)
measures.keyResult: greater pupil-size DECREASE (not increase) with higher usual physical-activity level (b=-.01, 95CI=-.01 to -.002, p=.008); -.024mm at high PA, -.016mm at moderate PA, ns at low PA; 13.9% variance explained -- disconfirms H4 in direction; authors caution the effect (~0.02mm) 'could hardly be distinguished from simple measurement error'

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: (a) first gaze location -- binary code for whether the first fixation landed on the active-stimulus side; (b) gaze duration -- relative percentage of viewing time on active vs. inactive stimuli
measures.apparatus: eye tracker (brand/model/sampling rate not specified in the extracted text); (a) logistic mixed model = attentional-orienting index; (b) linear mixed model = attentional-engagement index
measures.keyResult: first gaze: OR=1.14 increase per usual-PA unit (p=.012; significant at moderate OR=1.42 and high OR=1.61 PA, trend only at low PA OR=1.24 p=.065), 28.1% variance -- confirms H2; gaze duration: +7.8%/unit increase (p<.001; 20.2% longer at high PA, 12.4% at moderate PA, ns at low PA), 28.8% variance -- confirms H3

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.signal: reaction time (log-transformed) to detect a dot appearing where a physical-activity vs. physical-inactivity image had been
measures.apparatus: visual dot-probe task (adapted from MacLeod, Mathews, & Tata, 1986; stimuli from Kullmann et al., 2014); incorrect responses (0.9%) and RTs <200ms/>1500ms (0.4%) excluded; linear mixed model
measures.keyResult: dot-location x usual-PA interaction (b=-.02, p=.002): only high-PA participants (+1SD) detected the dot faster at the active-stimulus location (b=-.025, p=.003); no advantage at low/moderate PA; 40% variance explained (the study's largest R2) -- confirms H1; gaze duration (not first gaze or pupil dilation) also predicted this RT (p<.001, 36.3% variance)

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: usual moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (min/week); 2-item intention-to-be-active scale; confound questionnaire (hunger, thirst, PA current/previous day, sleep, caffeine, cigarettes)
measures.apparatus: adapted International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ; Craig et al., 2003)
measures.sampleN: 77 of 84 recruited (7 did not complete the PA questionnaire)
measures.keyResult: used as the continuous predictor/moderator for all other outcomes (not a boredom measure); usual PA = 199.3 min/week (SD 261.4); mean intention 7.6/10; active participants (34, 150min/week threshold) had higher intention and more/longer first-gaze and viewing-time toward physical-activity stimuli than inactive participants (43)

readings.claim: H1 confirmed conditionally: a two-way interaction between dot location and usual physical-activity level showed that only high-PA participants (+1SD) detected the dot faster at the active-stimulus location; low/moderate-PA participants showed no such advantage.
H2 confirmed conditionally: the odds of first-gazing at the active stimulus rose with usual physical-activity level, significant at moderate and high PA but only a trend at low PA.
H3 confirmed conditionally: relative viewing time toward active stimuli rose with usual physical-activity level, significant at moderate and high PA, not at low PA.

H4 disconfirmed in direction: participants showed a greater DECREASE (not increase) in pupil size viewing active stimuli as usual physical-activity level rose; the authors caution the effect is very small and could hardly be distinguished from measurement error.

Greater gaze duration (attentional engagement) predicted faster reaction times to detect the dot at the active-stimulus location, but neither first gaze nor pupil dilation did; pupil dilation showed only a marginal, gender-moderated (women-only) association with RT at the inactive-stimulus location.

The study names six limitations (self-report PA measure, correlational design, no neutral stimulus category, single-gender stimulus images, luminance uncontrolled, dot-probe task reliability/validity concerns) plus a design confound (prolonged sitting may have suppressed attraction to inactivity stimuli via outcome devaluation).

Attentional bias toward physical activity, observed here indirectly (RT) and directly (gaze), is read as evidence that automatic/impulsive processes -- not only reflective attitudes/intentions -- are involved in the regulation of physical-activity behavior.

tensions.axis: indirect (RT-based: Stroop, dot-probe) vs. direct (eye-tracking: first gaze, gaze duration) measurement of attentional bias
tensions.note: the paper's central methodological rationale: indirect RT measures are argued to be less reliable (Pennington et al., 2019), motivating the addition of direct gaze measures within the same design; both converge on similar conditional-on-PA-level patterns here, though the paper does not claim this generalizes.

tensions.axis: own hypothesis (H4: physical-activity stimuli evoke greater arousal/pupil dilation in active individuals) vs. own finding (smaller pupils = less arousal, for active individuals)
tensions.note: an internal, self-acknowledged tension: the result runs opposite to the hypothesized direction, and the authors explicitly caution that the (very small) effect could reflect measurement error rather than a genuine arousal-reduction phenomenon.

tensions.axis: this study's gender-null result vs. Berry, Spence, & Stolp's (2011) gender-moderated finding
tensions.note: Cheval et al. attribute the discrepancy to differences in control-stimulus content (Berry et al.'s control images carried gendered affective connotations; this study's images differed only in implied energy expenditure), qualifying rather than contesting the earlier finding.

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- eye-tracking / attentional-bias channel
dataset_channels.note: Cheval et al.'s three-tier eye-tracking design (first gaze for orienting, gaze duration for engagement, pupil dilation for arousal/value, all derived from one dot-probe paradigm and cross-validated against a behavioral RT measure) offers a reusable template for a future VR attention study's eye-tracking channel -- e.g., substituting 'engaging vs. boring/monotonous' VLE-content pairs for 'physical-activity vs. inactivity' image pairs and testing whether the same three indices track a trait-like predictor such as boredom proneness. The mapping is speculative and content-independent; the source itself never mentions boredom, VR, or education, and the dataset entry's own instrumentation is not yet confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).
